name: Algorithm Comparison / Best-Fit Selection
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai kaunsa sorting algorithm BEST/FASTEST/LOWEST-COMPLEXITY hai for a given scenario (or in general), ya specific algorithms ki complexities compare karni hain — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (22 me se 10 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: Recall the full comparison table (best/avg/worst, stable, in-place) directly — this is a memorization-and-lookup pattern, not a derivation one.
Check for special input structure mentioned (already sorted? small range? need stability?) and match to the table.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify what's being asked: worst-case? average-case? best-case? specific property (stable/in-place)?
2. Identify any special input structure given (sorted, reverse-sorted, few distinct values, range-bounded).
3. Match directly against the memorized comparison table.
variationsObserved: k sorted lists merge using heap — O(n log k), a specific derived application.
'Which needs the LEAST comparisons/swaps for THIS SPECIFIC array' — needs actual mental simulation of each candidate algorithm on the given small array, not just table lookup.
commonTraps: Reflexively answering 'Quick Sort' for 'fastest' without checking if WORST-CASE specifically is being asked (Quick Sort's worst case is O(n²), not the best choice there).

name: Comparison-Based Sorting Lower Bound (theoretical minimum comparisons)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai 'minimum number of comparisons needed to sort n elements' ya kisi specific n ke liye exact optimal comparison count — ye decision-tree/information-theoretic pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: General lower bound: Ω(n log n), specifically ⌈log2(n!)⌉ comparisons.
For small specific n, compute ⌈log2(n!)⌉ directly (e.g., n=5: log2(120)≈6.9, so 7).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For general asymptotic questions: answer Ω(n log n) directly.
2. For a SPECIFIC small n asking exact minimum comparisons: compute n!, then ⌈log2(n!)⌉.

3. For finding the kth smallest via decision tree (e.g., 1st, 2nd, 3rd smallest in a sorted matrix): reason about which comparisons are structurally forced vs avoidable given the existing partial order.
variationsObserved: Matrix with rows/columns already sorted — exploit the existing partial order to reduce comparisons below the naive bound for finding specific ranked elements.
commonTraps: Forgetting to round UP (ceiling) when computing ⌈log2(n!)⌉ for exact small-n answers.

name: Sorting Algorithm Property Definitions (stability, in-place)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai 'what does STABLE mean', ya matching-type question about which property belongs to which algorithm — pure definitional pattern.
whatShouldComeToMind: Stable = preserves relative order of EQUAL-valued elements.
In-place = O(1) (or O(log n) for recursion stack) extra space, no auxiliary array of size O(n).
generalSolvingApproach: 2. For matching-type questions, cross-reference against the memorized comparison table.
commonTraps: Confusing 'stable' with 'in-place' — these are independent properties (an algorithm can be one, both, or neither).

name: Trace a Specific Algorithm's Pass-by-Pass Behavior
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek specific array diya hai aur poocha hai kisi specific algorithm (Bubble/Insertion/Selection) ke KITNE PASSES ke baad array sorted ho jaayega, ya kitne swaps/comparisons honge — ye direct simulation pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Simulate the SPECIFIC named algorithm exactly as it's defined — don't substitute a different (even if faster) algorithm's logic.
Count comparisons and swaps SEPARATELY — they're often asked as distinct numbers.
conceptsRequired: Exact pass-by-pass mechanics of Bubble/Insertion/Selection Sort
generalSolvingApproach: 2. Simulate the named algorithm's exact procedure, one pass at a time, updating the array after each pass.
3. Count whatever is asked (passes to fully sort, total comparisons, total swaps) as you go.
variationsObserved: 'Distance to sorted' style questions (minimum replacements, not swaps, needed) — a different but related counting metric (longest increasing/matching subsequence idea).
commonTraps: Mixing up the mechanics of two different algorithms (e.g., applying Bubble Sort's adjacent-swap logic while asked about Selection Sort's find-minimum-then-swap logic).

name: Design an Optimal Algorithm for a Special-Case Sorting Scenario
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek special-structure sorting problem diya hai (jaise n distinct integers with n not known upfront, ya merging two sorted arrays optimally) aur poocha hai optimal algorithm design karo ya uski complexity batao — ye design pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Look for exploitable structure: is the array PARTIALLY sorted already? Are values RANGE-BOUNDED (enabling counting/radix sort)? Are there only a FEW distinct values (3-way partitioning)?
Merging two sorted arrays of size n each takes O(n) (NOT O(n log n)) via the standard two-pointer merge — a common 'obvious once you see it' result.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify what special structure the problem offers (bounded range, partial order, few distinct values, unknown size).
2. Match to a non-comparison-based or structure-exploiting technique if possible (counting sort, radix sort, merge).
3. Derive the complexity based on the chosen technique, not blindly assuming Ω(n log n) applies (it only applies to GENERAL comparison-based sorting).
variationsObserved: Sorting with only 3 distinct values (Dutch National Flag style problem) — achievable in O(n) with a single pass, no comparison-sort lower bound applies since there are only 3 possible values.
commonTraps: Assuming Ω(n log n) is an unbreakable barrier for EVERY sorting scenario — it only applies to general comparison-based sorting of arbitrary distinct values, not bounded-range or few-distinct-value scenarios.
